newsitem.title: INDIA: India storm-hit villagers weep as relief arrives.
newsitem.headline: India storm-hit villagers weep as relief arrives.

text.p: Rescue workers on Saturday sifted the rubble of thousands of homes on India's southeastern coast, searching for survivors two days after it was decimated by a cyclone.
Andhra Pradesh state officials said the toll had reached 477, but they feared more than 1,000 people may have died. Local newspapers and television fixed the toll higher, at 671.
On Saturday, vultures circled lazily over bloated cattle carcasses floating in a village canal swollen by floodwater.
Cyclone winds up to 180 kmph (110 mph) ravaged more than 800 villages, home to an estimated 2.5 million fishermen and farmers in an area known as the ricebowl of the state, officials said.

"I am at a loss for words to describe the tragedy in which about 1,000 people may have lost their lives," the Press Trust of India news agency quoted Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister V. Chandrababu Naidu as saying.
"All the thatched houses have collapsed and the roofs of tiled houses have blown off in the hurricane gales that swept the area," Naidu said.
"Most of the full-grown coconut trees have either collapsed or had their heads blown off."
Diwali, the most important festival in the Hindu calendar, falls next week. It will be bitter this year for the people of Rawlapalam, a hamlet in the heart of East Godavari.
East Godavari took the brunt of the cyclone. So far according to official figures an estimated 417 people are known to have died there.
Lakshmi, a 36-year-old labourer, said she and her family moved out of their thatched roof hut into a nearby brick and mortar construction to wait out the storm.
"When (the wind) started picking up speed and started howling, we got scared," Lakshmi told Reuters.
The wind became so destructive that the family did not dare venture out, she said. "The next morning I saw my hut totally razed to the ground and there was nothing left."
Almost 40 or 50 villages were still marooned after torrential rain and tidal waves had surged up to five kms (three miles) inland, officials said.
Police and troops struggled through swirling floodwaters up to three metres (10 feet) deep to reach other isolated hamlets.
"We are in the thick of cyclone work here," said R.V. Chandravadan, a magistrate in Rajahmundry, supervising rescue efforts at the heart of the devastation.

There has been no news from the submerged fishing hamlet of Bhairavpalem nearby, where 1,000 people made their living from netting shrimp. "There's no trace of the village," one official said. "It's out of contact."

The Eenadu newspaper reported more than 1,000 fishermen were missing. Officials said establishing accurate figures would be difficult as whole villages had been wiped out and tidal waters had scattered bodies.
"About 225,000 homes have been completely razed by the storm," a government official told Reuters.

About 615,000 hectares (1.5 million acres) of rice crops were destroyed, said H.S. Brahma, who is heading the relief operation. An additional 312,000 hectares (770,640 acres) of bananas, coconuts and sugarcane were devastated.

Television showed people wading waist deep through flood waters, overturned trucks, cars, uprooted trees strewn across roads and bodies trapped beneath trees that had crashed on to their fragile houses.
Villagers helped police parties clear away dozens of trees, chopping gnarled century-old banyan and tamarind trees into small logs.
Seven people were admitted to hospital with symptoms similar to cholera, the United News of India reported.
More than 400 teams of doctors and paramedics have spread out to innoculate villagers and spray disinfectant and insecticides to combat disease, relief official said.
Around 3.5 million people live in the fertile Konaseema region around the Godavari River delta. Andhra Pradesh's flat low-lying coastline leaves it vulnerable to tropical storms.

In 1977, more than 10,000 people were killed by a cyclone that drove a tidal wave up to 12 km (eight miles) inland. A cyclone killed 120 people in June this year, and 967 people died in another in 1990.
